Analyst reports say the data center battery market is 1.6B, 5.17B, and 7.5B at the same time—and all of them claim to be “right.”  

Think market sizing is a science with one true number? This quick guide shows why even “credible” forecasts can be billions apart—and how to turn that chaos into an advantage.

🔷 1) Define the market (or you’re already wrong): what’s in, what’s out  
– Every forecast starts with a hidden scope: are they counting just UPS batteries, all on-site energy storage, or every battery touching a data center power train?  
– Example: One firm may track only lithium-ion UPS in tier III–IV facilities, while another throws in grid-scale batteries supporting data centers plus VRFB pilot projects—same “market,” radically different totals.

🔷 2) Check the units and time anchors: apples vs. oranges  
– You must separate installed base, annual shipments, and total addressable market (TAM) and note whether numbers are nominal-year or constant-year dollars.  
– Example: 1.6B could be 2024 shipments at factory-gate prices, while 7.491B might be 2024 total installed fleet at end-user pricing with service contracts bundled in.

🔷 3) Deconstruct the forecast logic: assumptions > numbers  
– The real “truth” lives in the model: data center MW growth, battery penetration per MW, chemistries included, and replacement cycles (e.g., Li-ion swap every 8–10 years vs. lead-acid every 3–5).  
– Example: If one model assumes hyperscale AI load doubles battery demand per MW while another assumes “business as usual,” you can easily get a 3–5× spread by 2024–2026 even before debating price curves.

🔷 4) Turn conflicting reports into a strategic range, not a crisis  
– Treat each report as one scenario, then build a low/base/high range and map your own sales funnel, capacity plans, or fundraising story onto that band.  
– Example: Use 1.6B as a conservative annual demand floor and 7.5B as a bullish scenario—then stress-test hiring, manufacturing, and capital needs against both before locking your strategy.

🔷 5) Communicate honestly with stakeholders: show your math  
– Investors and execs are used to shaky market numbers; what they rarely see is a clear reconciliation and rationale.  
– Example: Instead of saying “The market is 7.5B,” say “Estimates range from 1.6–7.5B for 2024; here’s what’s included in each, and here’s why we’re planning against a 3–5B working range.”

That’s why mastering how to read and reconcile market forecasts isn’t optional—it’s the difference between betting your strategy on a single pretty slide and actually understanding your real opportunity.

Yesterday I said AI should be the doer and you should be the manager.
Managers train people.  Are you correctly training your ai assistants? do you even see them as YOUR assistant? ..........Most people don't and that's the whole problem.

 
Projects aren't new and plenty of you already use them. But nearly everyone is using one as a filing cabinet. A few documents chucked in, maybe a note about tone, and then confusion about why the output still reads like it was written for anybody.
 
A Project isn't storage. It's training.
 
Think about what actually happens when a trainee joins your desk.
 
You don't hand them a spec on day one and get annoyed when the shortlist is wrong. You tell them who you place and at what level. Which clients matter and why. What you turn down. You show them two cover sheets you were proud of so they know your standard rather than a generic one.
 
weeks later they're producing work that sounds like your desk, because you trained them properly.
 
That is exactly what Project knowledge does. Everything you put in it, every conversation inherits, forever.
 
Now the part people struggle with.
 
You don't actually know what to write in it. Not because you don't know your market. Because nobody has ever asked you the right questions about it.
 
So don't write it. Get interviewed.
 
Open a Project, and instead of dumping documents in, have Claude interview you and write the document itself.
 
Your market, properly. "Tech" isn't a market. "Backend engineers at Series A to C fintechs in London" is.
 
Who actually signs the contract, and whether that's the same person as the hiring manager, because it usually isn't.
 
Five real companies you've worked with or want to. Named. Then it looks them up and reads them back to you, and you find out whether your ICP is what you said it was.
 
Two or three real people, the kind you place and the kind you sell to.
 
The exact language your buyer uses when they're about to need you. This is the one that changes everything and nobody gets it first time. An agency owner writes "hiring a consultant" or "growing the desk". They never write "our tool spend is too high". Same signal, completely different words, and if you search the wrong ones you get career coaches instead of buyers.
 

Ten minutes of being asked questions from claude

Then get claude to create a "knowledge bank" of the anwers and all you do is add it into the context files.
 
Train it properly and it's consistent. Same as a trainee.
 
Now imagine that same assistant also has your LinkedIn, your enrichment tool, knows what CV stripping is, and can go and resource a live role.
 
That's when it stops being a chatbot and starts being someone on your team.

You manage hundreds of suppliers and thousands of SKUs. Your legacy systems were not built for machine learning. When leaders ask you to use AI, the goal is not a total transformation. The goal is solving specific problems.

Follow this framework to deploy AI without the chaos.

1. Find your biggest pain point
Do not look for every use case. Look for friction.
- Are supplier defects stopping your production lines?
- Does manual invoice matching cause payment delays?
- Do late deliveries make your planning unreliable?
Pick one area where manual work creates risk.

2. Measure your current state
You cannot prove value without a baseline. Track these metrics now:
- Average time to resolve invoice errors.
- Defect rates per supplier.
- Percentage of late deliveries.
- Cost of expedited freight.

3. Check your data
AI needs clean data. Audit your current landscape.
- Is your performance data in spreadsheets or buried in emails?
- Are your contracts digital or scanned PDFs?
- Do you have defect data linked to specific batches?
Data cleaning takes 40% to 60% of your implementation time. Plan for this.

4. Choose your path
- Build: High control but requires expensive data science talent.
- Buy: Fast deployment via platforms like Coupa or Ivalua.
- Partner: Custom models built by experts without hiring a full internal team.
Ensure any choice integrates with your existing ERP or QMS.

5. Run a pilot
Do not roll out AI to every supplier at once.
- Pick your top 20 suppliers or one specific plant.
- Set a 60 to 90 day window.
- Aim for specific goals, such as reducing late deliveries by 25%.
- Gather feedback from procurement and IT teams.

6. Govern and scale
AI is not a one-time project. Patterns shift and models drift.
- Create a process for when the AI predicts a delivery failure.
- Retrain models quarterly with new data.
- Once the pilot works, expand to more plants or new tasks like PO automation.

Winning with AI means treating it as a repeatable process, not a single technology project.

🚀 AI is an enhancer—but only for organisations that know how to deploy it.

The AI debate often starts with one question:

“How many jobs will AI replace?”

But there is another question businesses should be asking:

“How many more people can become productive when humans and AI work together?”

Deloitte South Asia is offering an interesting example.

According to reported comments by Nitin Kini, COO of Deloitte South Asia, the firm does not currently plan AI-driven layoffs and is targeting the hiring of 50,000 professionals in India this year.

If that strategy materialises, the message is significant:

AI adoption doesn't necessarily have to mean workforce reduction.

It can also mean workforce expansion + productivity improvement + capability transformation.

🧠 WHAT THIS APPROACH TELLS BUSINESS LEADERS

1️⃣ Upskilling over displacement

AI changes the value of skills.

Organisations that train employees to use AI effectively can potentially turn existing talent into significantly more capable talent.

2️⃣ Human + AI > Human or AI

AI can handle repetitive analysis, drafting, summarisation and pattern recognition.

Humans still bring:

🎯 Judgment
🤝 Relationships
🧠 Context
⚖️ Accountability
💡 Creativity
📈 Strategic decision-making

The opportunity is to redesign workflows around both.

3️⃣ Hiring doesn't disappear—it evolves

The demand may shift toward people who can combine domain expertise with AI literacy.

A lawyer who understands AI.

A finance professional who can automate analysis.

A marketer who can build AI-powered workflows.

An engineer who can collaborate with AI systems.

The competitive advantage increasingly becomes:

Domain expertise × AI capability.

⚠️ But there's an important caveat.

“AI won't cause layoffs” shouldn't become a universal prediction.

Different industries, companies and roles will experience very different effects.

Some jobs will be redesigned.

Some tasks will disappear.

Some new roles will emerge.

And some organisations may use productivity gains to reduce headcount.

The outcome depends on strategy, economics and execution.

💡 THE REAL FUTURE-OF-WORK QUESTION

The winners may not be companies that simply deploy the most AI.

They may be companies that figure out how to redesign work around AI while continuously upgrading their people.

AI should not simply make employees faster.

It should make organisations better.

👇 What is your organisation doing to prepare employees for AI—training, hiring, workflow redesign, or something else?

Back from a much-needed break and into a busy September for the Birmingham team. Thanks to the team for giving me the space to take a proper break.

What’s been good about coming back is the range of work and opportunity across our business.

A snapshot of what that looks like at the moment:

☁️ Cloud & Platform
Permanent and contract hiring, infrastructure change, hard-to-find engineering skills and project work where speed and delivery matter as much as long-term headcount.

🛡️ Cyber Security
Leadership, specialist hiring and contract capability, with more clients looking beyond filling a vacancy and at what their cyber function needs to become.

🤖 Data & AI
AI engineering, automation and data capability, alongside conversations about how organisations build teams around AI rather than treating it as a single hire.

💻 Software & Digital
Software engineering and leadership searches across very different environments, technology stacks and exciting greenfield builds.

🔄 Business Change & Transformation
Programme, project and change capability supporting wider technology transformation across permanent and flexible delivery models.

Then there’s everything between the specialisms.

🚀 Clients looking at Project Services and Statement of Work because what they really need is an outcome delivered.
🧑‍💻 Academy conversations where the answer might be developing capability rather than repeatedly competing for the same experienced talent.
🌍 Cross-border talent where widening the market creates options not available locally.
🎯 And plenty of straightforward recruitment where knowing the market properly still makes all the difference.

I’ve already got several meetings in the diary through September with clients old and new, and that’s probably the part I’m looking forward to most. Sitting down properly, understanding what they’re trying to build, where the gaps are and whether the answer is permanent hiring, contract, project capability or something else entirely.

If you’re looking at technology hiring or capability this autumn and want to engage the best talent with people who genuinely know their market, get in touch. I’d love to have a conversation.

From the ground, as a US nomad in Uganda, the global development job market can feel inaccessible, or pretty much unseen. Not sure if it's an algorithm thing, I do have a large and diverse community on #LinkedIn across expertise, geography, and sector.

Like many of you, I have spent the past 2 years rethinking and learning to shift my career after 25 years. And honestly, I refuse to see it as loss. 25 years working on global programs in Europe, the US, and parts of Africa should not go anywhere; it is what formed me into what I am today and the foundation I build the next chapter on.

Reorienting in your 50s takes real work, reframing what you know, unlearning and learning new vocabulary and skills, proving yourself in rooms you haven't been in before. It is hard, but it also feels like I am choosing my next move instead of just executing someone else's plan. Requires patience and constant interactions with people and organizations. Requires reminding people you are still interested for win-win collaborations. Requires to still offer a “pro-bono” demo to show what you can actually do beyond your fancy CV. We can write beautifully, we can talk, we say “yes, I can” but are we the DOers who inspire others, adapt constantly, and get the needed results. 

I see a lot of good resources, advice, and tools from people in my network (thank you all!). Still, as much as I can funnel, digest, and apply to my own situation the fact is simple: competition is high and the market is limited. 

Here's what I am noticing:

1. Volunteering/pro-bono service to demonstrate your capabilities makes it harder to later pitch it as paid work. 
2. Age is a factor everywhere, but especially on a continent with such a young, talented workforce.
3.  Decades of AID dependency and colonial history left a lasting assumption: Westerners, US citizens, show up with money, not skills to offer as a trusted peer. A mindset I have to work to move past in every relationship.
4. "Remote" increasingly means "remote, but in our time zone". I've seen regional African roles that are not based on the continent.
5.  Hiring processes are weaker, more biased, and no better with AI in the mix. From both sides, algorithms, writing, applying, vetting, selecting. Everyone seems tired of feeling stuck in a tech vortex with no human touch.

What is your take on the development job market from where you sit? What am I missing? I want to hear from my Ugandan and global peers.

I am open to consultancy work in social business and development. Remote, part-time, on contract, on call. Happy to have an informal call before any formal process if you think you might need someone with my experience, skills, and ability to adapt.

With all the noise around automation, AI calling and increasingly sophisticated outreach tools, I still think one of the biggest advantages you can have in a niche recruitment market is simply picking up the phone, speaking to the right people and actually listening.

Early in January, I called an architect in the US who was passively looking at the market. 

During the conversation, he mentioned that an Integration Architect had left his company around two months earlier and hadn't been replaced. It was starting to massively impact a project. 🎙️ 

After the call, I researched the team and found the architect who had left. 

That gave me a much better understanding of the gap they were trying to fill, particularly around MuleSoft and integration.  🧲 

I then went back through my network and identified three people who I thought could solve the problem: two contract options and one permanent.

I emailed the hiring manager initially and he opened the email once. No response.

I followed up with the three strongest profiles and explained why I thought they were relevant. That email was opened 31 times before he eventually replied asking for a call.

We filled the Integration Architect role, and that conversation subsequently led to another two hires within the wider team. 

In total, that original phone call generated around $75,000 in revenue.  💰  📈 

None of it would have happened if I hadn't spoken to someone in my market and listened carefully enough to pick up on a problem that wasn't being advertised as a live vacancy.

Listening gives you the information, but being able to connect that information to the right people and actually deliver against the problem is what opens the door.

AI can help you process information faster and automation can help you reach more people, but neither is much use if you don't understand what you're listening for.

Phone is king!  📱

I get asked about this a lot, and since it's my last week at Joko, I'm sharing my insights while everything is still fresh.

For months, hiring managers forwarded me recruitment agency contracts and asked me to review them. Is this clause standard? How does it compare to our usual terms? Where can we find a quick win that is easy for them but significant for us?
I would read the contracts, draw on my experience from working with several agencies, and provide a response. I was quietly pleased with that turnaround.

Then I paid attention to what I was actually doing, and it wasn't thinking. It was running a checklist. The same handful of questions, in the same order, on every contract. I had built that checklist myself, and then made myself the only way to reach it.

So I wrote it up properly and gave it to them.

The uncomfortable part is what that says about the year before. A good chunk of what made me feel useful was repeatable, and I had been performing it as judgement. That is not a pleasant thing to notice about your own job.

What happened next was better than I expected. The volume dropped, and the questions that still come to me are the ones the checklist can't answer: the genuinely odd clause, the case where the commercially sensible move and the legally safe move point in opposite directions. Those are the interesting ones. I used to reach them at the end of a day spent on the boring ones.

So this is the test I keep coming back to, and it has nothing to do with AI really. When someone asks you something, are you deciding, or are you executing a method you already have?

If it's the second one, they aren't asking for you. They're asking for the method, and you're standing in front of it.

Deploying AI in hiring and HR isn't just an operational efficiency decision—it's an escalating legal liability.
While corporate adoption of automated screening tools and generative AI assistants is surging, employment law experts are raising alarms over the hidden compliance traps organizations face.

In a recent analysis published via SHRM, labor and employment law firm Littler Mendelson examined the regulatory and litigation hazards emerging from everyday workplace AI use:

Key Compliance Risks & Legal Takeaways:

 * Algorithmic Disparate Impact: Automated resume parsers and candidate-ranking algorithms frequently introduce proxy discrimination by screening out candidates based on historical bias patterns. Under EEOC enforcement guidelines and local statutes (like NYC’s Automated Employment Decision Tool laws), employers—not software vendors—remain strictly accountable for discriminatory outcomes.

 * The "Shadow AI" Liability: Unregulated employee use of unsanctioned generative AI tools introduces significant trade secret leakage, data privacy breaches, and unverified work product into core business processes.

 * Auditability & Black-Box Decisions: When hiring or termination decisions involve algorithmic scoring, employers must be prepared to substantiate the business necessity and validity of the criteria in court if challenged.

 * Vendor Contract Deficits: Many enterprise SaaS agreements contain broad disclaimers that shift all regulatory compliance liability and bias risks onto the employer, leaving corporate legal departments exposed without contractual indemnification.
Practical Takeaway for Legal Counsel & HR Leaders:
Before rolling out recruitment or workplace AI tools, legal and HR teams must establish rigorous governance:

 * Conduct third-party bias audits on algorithmic hiring systems.
 * Update vendor contracts to mandate transparency and compliance warranties.
 * Implement enforceable enterprise AI use policies to govern employee tool usage.

Source: Littler Mendelson — What Legal Experts Need HR to Know About AI: Risks and Hazards

"Most HR departments are preparing for AI by automating tasks. They’re asking the wrong question."

​It’s not about how AI makes HR faster; it’s about how Agentic AI fundamentally rewrites the contract between human and digital labor.

​We are moving away from traditional headcount planning toward a co-intelligent, hybrid talent system. In this new reality, AI agents aren't just software tools; they are teammates.
​If HR remains stuck in transactional efficiency, the function will become obsolete. 

HR must step up as the architect of workforce transformation, leading across 6 vital pillars:

​📱1. Strategic Workforce Planning: "Task-Based, Not Role-Based."
​Forget static organigrams. Future workforce planning breaks jobs into task activities—routing work dynamically between humans, AI agents, and hybrid teams using real-time analytics.

​📐 2. Organizational Design: "Impact Over Hierarchy."
​Future-ready structures prioritize speed, outcome, and clear boundary lines. HR must lead scenario modeling and operating design that balances digital speed with unyielding human accountability.

​🎯 3. People Attraction: "Meta-Skills Rule."
​Hiring for fixed experience is dead. The priority shifts to meta-skills: learning agility, adaptability, and the capacity to co-create with digital agents.

​🔄 4. Hybrid L&D: "Learning in the Flow of Work."
​Continuous upskilling delivered by AI co-learners replacing static classroom training. Crucially, managers will now supervise, evaluate, and coach both humans and AI agents.

​📈 5. Talent Management: "Fluid & Outcome-Driven."
​Linear career ladders give way to hyper-personalized, outcome-focused trajectories. Incentive structures will directly reward successful human-AI collaboration and workflow innovation.

🫆​ 6. Employee Experience & Culture: "Safeguarding Trust.''
​As technology accelerates, the demand for human empathy, purpose, and trust surges. HR must embed AI ethics, preserve human dignity, and continuously monitor sentiment to maintain workplace trust.

​HR shouldn't wait for business transformation. HR must be the lighthouse, modeling agentic AI within its own operations first.

​Are you building an automated HR function, or are you architecting a co-intelligent workforce?

How Are U.S. Recruiting Agencies Surviving a Tougher Job Market?

The recruitment industry is facing a difficult equation: millions of job seekers, cautious employers, intense competition for openings, and growing pressure to control operating costs.

Yet recruiting agencies are adapting.

Some of these agencies have been forced to reduce their dependence on expensive physical offices and embracing remote or hybrid operations.

Others are investing in AI, Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) and virtual interviews to manage larger candidate pools more efficiently.

Many are strengthening relationships with employers by offering flexible staffing, specialized recruitment and workforce solutions.

The market is challenging, but it is not disappearing. The U.S. had 7.3 million job openings in July 2026, while temporary and contract staffing employment was 5.5% higher year-over-year in August, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and American Staffing Association.

The bigger question is:

Are recruitment agencies becoming more efficient, or are they simply being forced to reinvent themselves?

Perhaps the future of recruiting will be leaner, more digital, more specialized and increasingly remote.

Most companies hiring OTC support end up with someone who's good at one segment of the cycle and blind to how it connects to the rest. That gap is exactly where cash gets stuck and fraud gets missed.

🚨 URGENT HIRING – AI ARCHITECT | 12+ Years | CONTRACT 🚨
We are looking for an experienced AI Architect to join an exciting enterprise technology project involving Cloud, AI/ML, GenAI, and modern application architecture.
🔹 Position: AI Architect
🔹 Experience: 12+ Years
🔹 Location: Remote
🔹 Contract: 6 Months
🔹 Budget: ₹1.65 LPM
🔹 Shift: 2:00 PM – 11:00 PM IST
🔹 Hiring Type: Contract
🔹 UAN: Mandatory & will be validated
📍 Face-to-Face Interview:
Candidates must be available to travel for 1 day for an F2F interview at any one of these locations:
Gurugram | Pune | Bengaluru | Hyderabad | Chennai | Bhopal | Jaipur
🔑 Key Skills & Expertise
✅ 12+ years in end-to-end application development & architecture
✅ Strong AWS Cloud expertise – EC2, S3, Lambda, RDS, ROSA
✅ AI/ML & GenAI Architecture
✅ LLM integration, Agentic AI & AI-powered solutions
✅ AWS Bedrock, SageMaker & AgentCore
✅ Microservices, Docker & Kubernetes
✅ Terraform / AWS CloudFormation
✅ CI/CD & DevOps practices
✅ Application Security & 12-Factor principles
✅ Enterprise architecture, system design & technology strategy
✅ Experience with LangChain / LangGraph / AWS Strands / Google ADK is a plus
✅ Knowledge of MCP-based integrations, RAG & multi-agent orchestration is preferred
🎯 Preferred: AWS Solutions Architect Professional / AWS DevOps Engineer Professional certification and experience in airline technology environments.
📩 Interested candidates: Please share your updated resume along with:
Total Experience
Relevant AI/Architecture Experience
Current Location
Expected Rate
Notice Period
UAN Availability
⚡ Immediate Joiners / Short Notice Candidates will be preferred.

Mail ID:career@codingera.in
